t: How Long Should It Take to Reach Consensus
q: The downside of consensus is that it takes time. The more people involved with input or advocacy, the longer consensus-making takes.
Self-interested team members who know this sometimes block a decision they don’t like by resisting the wisdom of the group and asking for more data, analysis, and discussion.
Before beginning the decision process, good leaders and organizations set a deadline by which consensus must be achieved.
As a rule, teams prefer to reach consensus through compromise rather than lose the right to make the decision.
Allowing any individual to stand in the way of decision-making guarantees ineffectiveness.

t: The Authenticity Myth
q: The contemporary view is that authenticity is about openly sharing the true self through words and actions.
Authenticity as openness and transparency is a myth that can get leaders into big trouble.
Authenticity is more accurately defined as what a leader does the most often.
We know leaders for what they do consistently, not for what they say they believe or value.
Who you truly are is reflected by what you do, not by how open or disclosive you are about what you believe or think.

t: Research Bite #39: Investigating the impact of Accessible Pedagogies on the experiences and engagement of students with language and/or attentional difficulties
q: This academic paper explores the impact of Accessible Pedagogies™ on the classroom experiences and engagement of Year 10 students with language and/or attentional difficulties in Australia.
Reducing extraneous language and cognitive load in their teaching significantly boosts cognitive engagement for students with language and/or attentional difficulties.

Extraneous Language and Cognitive Load: Instructional barriers, such as long, complex instructions or superfluous teacher talk, that burden students' working memory and language comprehension systems.

Long, complex instructions, abstract language, unnecessary teacher talk, low-frequency words, and fast-paced verbal instruction can create significant barriers for students, especially those with ADHD and Developmental Language Disorder (DLD).

Findings suggest that the reduction of extraneous language and cognitive load through teachers' use of Accessible Pedagogies™ may have helped students deploy available mental effort to engage in learning, rather than expend that effort to overcome unnecessary instructional barriers

the quantitative findings on student engagement relied on a very small sample size (e.g., 10 students in the intervention group), which the study itself acknowledges "did constrain quantitative analyses".

t: How Consumed by Social Comparison Are You
q: In small doses, social comparison allows people to benchmark their skills and talents against others to get better.
Excessive social comparison, whether it springs from jealousy or a need to be viewed as more successful than others, produces feelings of inadequacy and anxiety
Research proves that the idealized images of others’ lives and successes promoted on social media heighten personal dissatisfaction and emotional distress.
Smart people come to the realization that the comparison game is unwinnable—there is always someone more skilled, more accomplished, and more polished.
The best leaders keep their eyes down and attend to their own advancement.

t: What Leaders Can Learn From the College Football Quarterback Whisperer
q: He coached a walk-on named Baker Mayfield, who dominated in college, won the Heisman Trophy, and now quarterbacks the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
Morris knows how to take unheralded football prospects and mold them into top-tier quarterbacks.
He develops a player’s mental acuity to see the field, process defensive schemes, and adapt under pressure.
He believes that taking situations apart and examining every detail helps his quarterbacks to develop a “football brain,” the ability to process fast, decide fast, and execute with confidence.
This big-picture thinking is developed from dissecting many situations with two simple questions: “What is happening?” and “Why?

t: When Teacher Training Feels Like a Sales Pitch (and How to Push Back)
q: Certain approaches were presented as the only right ones. Others were brushed aside with a dismissive label.
The problem is that “research says” is sometimes used to make an idea sound more authoritative than it really is.
Paul Kirschner and Mirjam Neelen refer to this as eminence-based education. The problem? It discourages questions.

Retrieval practice and explicit instruction, for example, are highly effective for novice learners (Agarwal, Nunes, & Blunt, 2021; Kirschner, Sweller, & Clark, 2006). Yet if you say you use retrieval practice, you risk being accused of “drill and kill.
Sometimes practices criticized as inequitable, like explicit instruction, have in fact been shown to support struggling learners (Hattie, 2009; Stockard et al., 2018).
Pushing back doesn’t mean being combative. It means keeping the dialogue honest, evidence-informed, and centred on student learning.

t: Incremental Fact Fluency
q: If students don't seem to make progress with a skill, a good strategy is to take that skill, break it down into smaller pieces, focus on one piece at a time, and gradually build up to the larger skill.
It's called "incremental rehearsal." Incremental rehearsal is a strategy for students who are struggling to learn their math facts.
I think the biggest cause of math anxiety is being asked to do something over and over, yet feeling like you're not getting better at it.
I generated these using AI. I've checked them and I don't think there are any mistakes, but I could be wrong.
I literally needed dozens of attempts before the AI could get the handout right. I prompted multiple different LLMs over and over again.
For math facts, that means breaking the facts down into smaller groups and gradually expanding the pool of facts that students can retrieve from memory.

t: How To Allow For Open Class Discussion
q: This is a great question because at first glance our classroom management plans don’t allow for open, back-and-forth interaction among students and teacher.
The answer is that it does leave room. You can indeed conduct free-flowing conversation in your classroom while still maintaining the integrity of the rule.
Give it a name, like “open discussion time.” Define precisely what it is and why it’s good for the class.
For open discussion to work, your students need to have the skills to navigate its jazz-like flow.
Try five minutes and choose simple, relatable topics like, for example, why mint chip ice cream is so popular.

t: Compliance and the Deterrence of Checking
q: Sometimes, even a minor violation can impact the integrity, safety, and legal standing of the organization.
The mere possibility and expectation of compliance checks act as a deterrent to rule-breaking behavior.
Research has consistently shown that random or regular monitoring is a stronger deterrent than the severity of whatever the punishment might be.
The simple existence of a system acts as a deterrence against rule-breaking and cutting corners.
The idea is not to block every shot. The idea is to make your opponent believe that you might block every shot.

t: Can AI Help With Formative Assessment?
q: They don't have a model of cognition. They don't know what it is the students are thinking.
No matter how experienced the teacher, formative assessment always runs into the same problem: diagnosis at scale.

LLMs may indeed operate only as probabilistic models over text. They may not possess a model of cognition. But, as with teachers, I think the functional test is a behavioural one: does the system act as if it has a useful cognitive model?
In theory, LLMs could access everything educators have ever written about teaching: examiner reports, guides, textbooks, research papers, and online forums. This is collective PCK at scale.
Overall, the LLM performed well in diagnosing misconceptions in the pieces of work I gave it, particularly in the structured domains of maths, science, and languages.
The teacher still sets pacing and pedagogy. The model handles the piece best done as one-to-one diagnostic marking, for situations where a mini-whiteboard can’t tell the whole story.

t: 3-Read Friday #84: AI Formative Assessment, Teacher Training Pitfalls, and Fact Fluency
q: Becky describes a fascinating experience she had. She wrote a simple prompt (which she shares in the post) that enabled a freely available LLM to analyse a photo of students' work, identify possible misconceptions, and then write diagnostic questions to find more evidence for those misconceptions.
Jim and Nihdi take a deep dive into the world of teacher CPD, offering five warning signs to look out for, and actions you can take as recipients of that CPD.
I'll admit to falling foul of the first one on their list myself.
Regular readers know I love a bit of AI Maths resource creation. So, I loved Dylan’s post about a series of worksheets he has created using AI to help students develop fluency in their times tables.
Check out my brand-new 16-part book series, The Tips for Teachers guide to.

t: Do You Work in a Take Credit or Share Credit Culture
q: Some organizations are Take Credit workplaces, where, as long as the team member or team doesn’t go too far, it is perfectly acceptable and expected to tout good outcomes and results.
Other organizations are Share Credit workplaces, where it is considered bad form to claim individual responsibility for positive results.
Colleagues don’t always tell others they are violating the cultural norm regarding sharing or taking credit.
This can have a devastating effect on a team member’s trajectory and acceptance.
For long-term success, follow their lead. In the end, the best self-promotion matches the expectations and practices of your trusted colleagues.

t: Three Questions Leaders Must Answer Before Delegating a Decision
q: These are generally referred to as two-way decisions, meaning they are important but can be reversed and changed without significant disruption or discomfort to the team or organization.
Pushing down decisions to others is not only expedient but also necessary for developing other leaders.
To assist them with decision delegation, the best leaders ask and answer three foundational questions regarding any two-way decision they do not want to control.
With that limited guidance, the delegated decision-maker is set up for success.
More than half the battle of making a quality decision comes down to who is making it and who else is weighing in.

t: Diagnostic Questions: Is There Value in Just One? tonmaths.com/resourcesnew/8.%20Research/Formative%20Assessment/Is%20there%20value%20in %20just%20one%20-%20Dylan%20Wiliam%202006.pdf
q: Teachers can use single, high-quality questions to make quick decisions about what students understand and to adjust their teaching to meet students' learning needs.

This is called a “decision-pull” approach to data-driven instruction, and it contrasts with the “data-push” approach where teachers are given large amounts of data that they may not have time to use or may not find helpful.

In addition to being easy to collect, good decision-pull questions should also have incorrect answers that help teachers understand what students do not understand and provide ideas about what to do about it.

While the reliability of a single question is lower than the reliability of a test with multiple questions, a single question can still provide enough information to guide instruction in real-time, especially if the question is well-chosen.
Teachers who collect information about student achievement but are unable to do anything with that information get worse results than teachers who do not collect such information at all.
While the accuracy of a decision based on a single item may be far from perfect, it is better than a decision based on no data at all.

t: The Tires I Fix
q: I'm not a mechanic, but I can change a flat tire. I don't know how to fix a transmission or build an engine, but if you're stranded on the side of the road with a popped tire, I got you.

My work as a writer is a lot like that. I can’t figure out how to overhaul the school system to make it better. (I mean, except for four-day schoolweeks… .) But, I can help with a few basic problems: Overwhelm (for teachers, administrators, students); Demotivation (for teachers, admin, students); Clarity.

Moments of Genuine Connection. This is the operating system of a well-functioning classroom. Stop leaving care signals to chance, start peacefully and systematically ensuring that every student knows that you see, value, and know them.

Mini-Sermons. No one is better situated to speak to the Value of the courses I teach than me. Not parents, not administrators, not the culture. I know all the ways in which my subject is good and its work is worthwhile.
Every educator has experienced bad professional development, and that’s because creating enjoyable and productive professional development experiences is hard stuff.

The genius of John Wooden wasn’t in accruing more championship rings than he could fit on one hand; it was in breaking basketball down into its smallest pieces and making these pieces crystal clear for his students.

t: Research Bite #38: The Memory Paradox: Why Our Brains Need Knowledge in an Age of AI
q: over-reliance on external tools and AI for information storage is leading to a decline in human cognitive abilities, evidenced by the reversal of the Flynn Effect.
underuse of declarative and procedural memory systems hinders reasoning, impedes learning, and reduces productivity by preventing the formation of robust internal knowledge structures
In a world where we can look up almost everything, the ironic truth is that the knowledge we carry inside our heads is more valuable than ever
Teachers should recognize that memorizing basic facts, vocabulary, and formulas is crucial for building robust mental frameworks (schemata) and developing true expertise.

Constant reliance on external aids can lead to "biological pointers" (remembering where to find information) instead of actual knowledge, creating an "illusion of knowledge" that undermines deep understanding.
Encourage students to grapple productively with challenges before seeking help, aiming for an optimal 85% success rate.

t: Lets Eliminate the Bureaucracy Together
q: Team members experience unnecessary rules, outdated processes, and redundant layers of approvals all day long.
After the CEO requested team members to send in suggestions via email, the company received 1500 recommendations and used them to change more than 450 of their processes based on the feedback.
Describing exactly what suggestions the enterprise is looking to eliminate with examples prevents people from making wild recommendations
Lastly, in many cases, the eliminated process must be replaced by something else less burdensome and more streamlined.
Bureaucracy defends the status quo long past the time when the quo has lost its status.

t: Letting Others Think They Are Right Says a Lot About Your Emotional Intelligence
q: Letting others think they are right is a wise move in many situations. Especially when being “right” is less important or totally unimportant.
Allowing others to believe they are right privileges the relationship over accuracy and illustrates that the leader cares as much about harmony as they do about correctness.
Smart leaders conserve their strong advocacy for more meaningful topics and issues.
In fact, when personal safety is at stake, letting others believe they are right can be dangerous.
Good leaders prefer harmony over truth when the consequences are insignificant.

t: Vividly Visualize Accomplishments the Team Is Far From Attaining
q: By visualizing the accomplishment, even those far in the distance, leaders turn abstract and wishful goals into expectations and intentions.
The more vivid the visual, the more engaged people become. Good leaders make the pathway to success vividly clear.
He insisted they do this in early team practices so they could visualize the pride and satisfaction of what winning would feel like.
Visualizing successful completion highlights the significance and meaning of success.
If the goal is big and meaty, visualizing the accomplishment will help align the team and inspire engagement and action.

t: Why You Must Tell Your Students WHY
q: If this has ever happened to you, then you know how hard it is to nod off amidst the cleaning crew’s toils and blaring announcements over the intercom.
His answer: “Because I’m the security guard and you don’t need to know.
In other words, it was arbitrary. This, of course, infuriated the horde, who one after the other trudged back to the gate muttering indecents under their breath.
If you don’t have a compelling reason why you do, well, everything—though especially your rules, expectations, and policies—then you shouldn’t do it.
So what is a compelling reason? Whatever is best for students, which then must be explained to them in a way they understand.
The result is better motivation and a more influential relationship with your class.

t: Which Multimedia Strategies Actually Improve Learning?
q: If I was to sum up his work in one idea, it’s that clarity beats novelty, and that students learn by actually thinking hard about stuff, not merely being entertained.
Pooling Mayer’s studies from 1990–2022, the average impact is a respectable “medium” (g=0.37).

Text combined with diagrams emerged as the most reliable approach across all learning outcomes. This humble combination consistently produced meaningful learning gains whether students were trying to memorise facts, make inferences, or transfer knowledge to new situations.
Virtual reality, despite generating enormous excitement and investment, VR showed non-significant effects overall.
The decline in effect sizes over time is particularly sobering, suggesting that as multimedia becomes commonplace, its advantages may diminish.
For me, this research joins a growing body of evidence suggesting that educational technology's benefits have been oversold.

t: The Hidden Lives of Teachers
q: One of his most enduring ideas is that beneath every classroom lie three hidden worlds. There is the teacher’s world, where lessons are carefully planned and delivered.
When I first began delivering my Middle Leadership Mastery course, I found myself adding a fourth hidden world: the teacher’s world of beliefs, values and internal narratives.
A piece of feedback might be heard as encouragement by one teacher, but as criticism by another.
If we ignore this hidden world, professional development can miss its mark. Leaders may deliver the same message, but teachers will interpret it in very different ways.
That is why effective CPD cannot just be about presenting strategies. It must also create space for reflection, discussion or coaching that surfaces the teacher’s hidden world.
It is in this world, of beliefs, values and interpretations, that the success of CPD is often decided.

t: Principles of Effective Prison Work
q: Effective prison work means making a series of choices under pressure – officers select, adapt, and switch strategies to achieve their goals.
Procedural justice means that decisions are made in ways that are visibly fair. To achieve this, prisoners must know why and how a decision was made, and what informed it.

A transformative prison officer will look to use the momentary interaction as they lock prisoners away as a chance to help prisoners rethink their actions, choose fresh goals, commit to change, and act on their commitments.
We combine clear, firm boundaries with a warm, caring approach. Firm boundaries are crucial in keeping the prison safe, maintaining consistent rules, and helping prisoners behave appropriately.
Whenever discretion is exercised, the risk is that an exception today becomes an expectation tomorrow.
The more officers can be consistent in the way they meet individuals’ needs, the clearer expectations are for prisoners and officers alike.

t: Getting People Comfortable With a Decision They Think Is Wrong
q: Getting comfortable with an unpopular or detrimental decision can be extremely difficult for people.
By taking responsibility for their discomfort, good leaders flip the script and promote acceptance of the decision.
The critical move is to engage the disappointed colleague with a simple question: What can I do to get you more comfortable with the decision?
Sometimes it is not the help but the desire to help that soothes hard feelings.
Placing the burden of their discomfort partially on your shoulders as a leader will likely change how they view both you and the decision.

t: 3-Read Friday #83: Effective Prison Work, Multimedia Learning, and the Hidden Lives of Teachers
q: Something different from Harry - a deep dive into effective prison work: practical ways to communicate effectively, manage conflict, and promote change. I will leave you to decide how many transfer to the classroom.
Carl takes a customery deep dive into a new meta-analysis of Richard Meyer’s multimedia principles.
Carl picks out the principles of design that are likely to have the most impact on student learning, and identifies the boundary conditions that can make or break them.

Graham Nuttall's book, The Hidden Lives of Learners, had a massive impact on my teaching. Nuttall identifies three hidden worlds within our classrooms: the teacher's world, the peer world, and the private world.
In this post, Adam adds a fourth world: the teacher's world of beliefs, values and internal narratives.

t: Leveling the Playing Field: Attention Mitigates the Effects of Intelligence on Memory e-on-memory/ -- original paper:
q: This study explores how attention influences memory encoding in children and adolescents, specifically examining the impact of different attentional mechanisms.
Their findings indicate that engaging suppression during learning significantly enhances recognition memory, even counteracting the effects of individual differences in intelligence (IQ).

When only basic orienting was present, IQ was the primary predictor of memory performance, but suppression mechanisms proved crucial for boosting memory accuracy, particularly for participants with lower IQs.
Engaging selection via suppression is particularly impactful because it counteracts individual differences in intelligence.

The study found that simply spending the same amount of time looking at target items did not guarantee equal encoding efficacy; the underlying attentional mechanism (facilitation vs. suppression) was critical.
Specifically, we show that selection mechanisms involving suppression have the power to boost memory encoding, effectively counteracting individual differences in intelligence.

t: How Important Is This to You
q: Conflicts, large and small, are born from one party not giving an issue of great importance to the other party the gravity they believe it deserves.
When people bring issues to your attention to discuss or resolve, it’s a good idea to ask them this question before attending to it: How important is this to you?
Good leaders make whatever is important to you important to them.
The default of asking these questions signals genuine respect and interest in others and encourages people to share openly about what they expect.
By not taking the issue seriously, the other party saw your actions (or lack thereof) as symbolic of the relationship.

t: Attention, Mindwandering, and Mood ://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10073349/1/Hobbiss_Attention%2C%20mindwandering%2C%20and%2 0mood_AAM.pdf
q: The provided text explores the relationship between attention focus, mind-wandering, external distractions, and reported happiness levels through two studies involving 524 participants.
The researchers hypothesize that both mind-wandering and external distractions stem from a common state of reduced attention focus.

The studies revealed a significant negative association between both mind-wandering and mobile phone distractions and reported happiness, suggesting that a reduced ability to maintain attention may have emotional consequences.
Mobile phones are identified as a prevalent source of external distraction and are significantly linked to reduced happiness.

Longer proportional durations of mindwandering and external distractions are linked to reduced mood. This implies that persistent, prolonged periods of inattention are particularly detrimental, and teachers should be attuned to signs of sustained disengagement.
The results are consistent with the hypothesis that a state of reduced attention focus underlies both mindwandering and distractibility and clarify the link with happiness.

t: Realizing That You Have Been Taken Advantage Of
q: A colleague or friend who never reciprocates. Scant communication or follow-up after you’ve helped someone out.
Once you realize you have been taken advantage of, the imperative question is what to do about it.
Describe the relationship you want to have as opposed to complaining about what has already transpired. Ask them to think along with you about ways to address the disparity you are feeling.
In the instance of someone taking credit for your ideas or results, document your accomplishments and proposals in emails and share them widely, including with the guilty party.
Good people take advantage of opportunities, not other people. That’s how you know they’re good people.

t: Lets Talk Sustainable Teacher-Student Relationships
q: I’m the last person that’s going to tell you school is all about relationships. Because it’s not. It’s all about advancing the long-term flourishing of young people by teaching them to master things that, apart from school, they’d be unlikely to master.

few factors are as critical to long-term student and teacher flourishing as good, working relationships between educators and students. And when you’re a secondary teacher working with 100+ kids… building those relationships is a tall order.

MGCs are a special kind of strategy: I can explain the what/why/how to you in just a moment or two — so simple — but here I am, thousands of MGCs into my career, and I’m still learning, tweaking, adjusting, and improving — so deep.
And in the past couple years, I’ve been blown away by how complex it is to get whole schools to adopt and gain proficiency at something so basic.
I’ll discuss how I’ve found MGCs to deepen my soul and expand my experience of the goodness of life (sounds cheesy, but it’s true).
I’ll share what works best in getting MGCs installed at the baseline “this is who we are, this is what we do” level of faculty culture.

t: Leading People Who Are in Denial
q: They refuse to accept any reality or facts that make them too uncomfortable. To preserve their self-image and to avoid shame or anxiety, they vehemently disallow any acknowledgment of a pattern known well to others.
Many leaders have learned the hard way that simply confronting those in denial with the facts usually makes matters worse.
What makes the situation even harder is the fact that many people in denial are empowered to do so by others.
By becoming a living example of the flawed behavior or pattern, a leader lets the action speak for them, often without any commentary.
In addition to the negative effect an unaddressed dysfunction has on others, living in denial stalls personal growth and escalates conflicts in relationships.

t: Research Bite #37: Prior knowledge activation as preparation prior to instruction
q: This research investigates how activating prior knowledge prepares secondary school students for learning new concepts within two-phase instructional designs like Productive Failure (PF) and Vicarious Failure (VF).

the findings suggest that activating some relevant knowledge is sufficient for preparation, even if it doesn't encompass all aspects of the target concept, benefiting students across all levels of initial prior knowledge.
Activating some relevant prior knowledge before instruction is beneficial for students of all levels of prior knowledge.
This paper provides first causal empirical evidence on the conditions under which intermediate knowledge facilitates students' learning from instruction.
Activating some relevant knowledge can prepare students for subsequent instruction and benefit students of all levels of prior knowledge
the experimental conditions' differences might have been too small, as both included crucial prerequisite components, possibly yielding similar outcomes.

t: Do You Have Mission Charisma
q: What both sets of leaders must have in common is mission charisma.
Their conviction and commitment to the mission and vision bring out a higher gear.

Not everyone has personality-driven charisma, but almost any leader can get excited, in their own way, to project a mission-centric charisma of enthusiasm, passion, and commitment about the center spoke of what makes the organization great.
It's a welcome offset to the common drawback of charismatic leaders who are known to focus too much of their attention on their own self-interests over that of the team.
A good leader doesn’t have to be smooth, charming, or outgoing. But they must be able to express that the mission and vision really matter to them. Intensely so.

t: Unlearning Is an Important Part of Learning
q: Letting go of outdated beliefs, inaccurate opinions, and unproductive habits makes room for new ideas and practices.
Unlearning isn’t about forgetting. It is about reevaluating and replacing.
Identifying what needs to be unlearned is the biggest challenge. Even highly self-aware leaders are unlikely to know what they need to unlearn.
That’s why third parties, such as executive coaches and mentors, can play such a pivotal role in the process.
The best leaders learn, unlearn, and relearn. They know self-improvement and quality decision-making depend on it.

t: Start the Next Project Immediately
q: Staring at a blank screen or piece of paper is among the most painful of creative challenges. Inertia and writer’s block between assignments can affect even the most skilled practitioners.
That’s why so many writers, artists, and performers advise practitioners to start the next project immediately after finishing the last one.
Once the new project has been started, the practitioner can now take a break and allow the brain to rest, recharge, and incubate new ideas.
Creativity muscles and conditioning are much like physical ones. Breaking off from the work for more than a few days makes starting again painful and slow.
As a wise person once said, “The secret of getting ahead is getting started.

t: Reframing Success
q: When students achieve full marks without effort, or when they sail through an activity without really thinking, the success is shallow.
As Paul Kirschner says, learning is a change in long-term memory.

Robert Bjork’s concept of desirable difficulties is helpful here. When students are asked to engage in effortful retrieval, when they grapple with concepts and experience some struggle, the learning becomes more durable.
A student who always gets one hundred percent without effort does not truly experience competence, because they have not had to struggle and overcome anything.
I have made the mistake of relying on these surface-level questions to prepare my students for assessments when the goal should be on long-term learning.
We show them that success is not about perfection today, but about growth tomorrow.

t: Managing the Room
q: Robert Frisch, in Who’s in the Room (2011), reminds us that many leadership struggles do not stem from poor strategy at all, but from poorly managed rooms.
A "decision-making" meeting dissolves into open-ended talk. A "discussion" meeting is remembered as a decision, until someone reverses it later.
Frisch’s central insight is deceptively simple: managing the room requires being explicit.
Better to say, “This decision does not require your presence,” than to offer false inclusion. Clarity is kinder than token invitations.
Middle leaders, key agents of changes in schools, are particularly vulnerable to the costs of poorly managed rooms.
Because in the end, the quality of leadership is measured not in lofty statements, but in the lived experience of a room.

t: A Team Member Repairing a Damaged Reputation Needs to Make a Sacrifice
q: It takes years to build a solid reputation on a team. But only minutes to destroy it.
Team members serious about reestablishing their credibility must first own the mistake or set of bad actions and issue an apology to the team and the leader.
Consistency in behavior, attitude, and engagement will eventually replace the damaged reputation with a new and better one if the team member can avoid any new mishaps.
Repairing a damaged reputation nearly always benefits from a sacrifice to prove how serious the offender is in making a fresh start.

Sacrifice communicates a real shift in priorities, demonstrating with actions, not words, that the team’s success and trust are of the highest importance. The greater the sacrifice, the more likely the team will forgive and forget over time.

t: 3-Read Friday #82: Digital Attention, Managing the Room, and Reframing Success
q: Daniel asks whether the recent trend in the US - and in the UK - for schools to ban mobile phones will solve the problem of reducing student distraction, or has the long-term use of digital technologies rendered many students unable to sustain their focus?
This is a post that should be mandatory reading for all senior leaders who organise meetings.
Nimish shares Robert Frisch’s core insights about being explicit and stage-setting to ensure that leaders don’t waste any of their team’s precious time.

In much the same way as the Bjorks distinguish between performance and learning, Jo warns against a focus on short-term measures of success (lots of lovely ticks in books), and instead suggests ways we can help students achieve and feel successful for the long term.
Primary teachers, have you seen our brand-new White Rose maths collection of diagnostic questions? Reception to Year 6, all free, available here.

t: The Insanity of Preparing Students for Jobs That Dont Exist Yet by Using Unproven Methods and Ignoring Fundamentals nproven-methods-and-ignoring-fundamentals
q: Strangely enough, it sometimes feels like what is lost in many supposed leaps forward in education is the basics of learning. From a cognitive perspective, we’re being pushed away from what works in order to prepare students for ‘work that doesn’t exist yet.

If we don’t know of the work our students will be doing when they are out in the workforce, then how can we predict that we’re not preparing them for that unknown world? And how do we know what we should do to prepare them?

reading, writing, and mathematics are predicted to be ‘out of focus’ in 2030; they are less essential now and not expected to increase in use. Wait…what? How it the world will the ability to read and write and perform mathematical computations be less essential?
You cannot be creative with information you don’t have. There’s got to be some understanding and memory of a topic in order to successfully create from that subject.
it’s not a long article (love it), but it’s packed with wisdom. That’s basically the goal here in DSJ Land, but I can’t make the points Blake makes any better than he does.

t: How To Encourage Difficult Students
q: One of the best things you can do for difficult students is put a stop to the years of false praise they’ve been showered with.
Not a good hour or even a good day. Your praise must be in response to actual leveling up of behavior.
That’s it. Simple. Matter-of-fact. Don’t be effusive or over-the-top. Tell them the truth, nothing more.
But again, you can’t be emotional. Your words and tone mustn’t be babyish or condescending.
The prickly pears need you to never give up on them. They need you desperately to see it through for their long-term future, regardless of how long it takes.

t: Be Careful About How You Ask Your Leader for Advice
q: Leaders naturally like to be asked what they think and enjoy the respect and deference they feel when asked for their opinion.
Nothing is more insulting to a leader than asking for an opinion and then ignoring it. So, it is more strategic to solicit a broader view.
Ideally, it is best not to ask leaders to opine about specific options or choices. Once they land on a preferred option, the team member now faces a directive disguised as advice.

If, by chance, the leader insists on giving specific guidance in the form of a plan or action, then it is important for the team member to instantly thank them and to respond that it is worth considering, without committing to it.
By asking for a more general discussion of the problem and their experience in tackling it, team members can avoid being tied to a specific option or choice. It’s all in how you ask the question.

t: Avoiding the Zebra Retreat
q: A Zebra Retreat is a term from medical decision-making that describes the tendency for doctors to shy away from pursuing a rare diagnosis (the “zebra”) even when the evidence strongly points to it as a possibility.
Decision-makers of all stripes (pun intended) prefer not to consider isolated, unconventional, or innovative options, and often retreat from them to avoid being viewed as crackpots or eccentrics.
This bias can suppress innovation and prevent organizations from capitalizing on emerging opportunities, instead favoring incremental improvement and mimicking competitors.
Simply knowing the leader has an appetite for less conventional solutions goes a long way to relieve the pressure to conform.
There’s no limit to how much you’ll know, depending on how far beyond zebra you go.

t: Even When an Extreme Response Is Justified, Retaliation Is Judged More Harshly
q: Here’s the surprising fact: In all walks of life, the retaliator and not the offender commonly garners the negative press.
Whereas a thoughtful response can demonstrate emotional maturity, a retaliatory one is viewed as an emotional reaction, unbecoming of a leader.
Retaliation that is planned rather than spontaneous can draw even more attention and derision from parties outside of the conflict.
The only exception to this rule occurs when retaliation is viewed as a sacrifice or a protection for others. Then the retaliator is given a pass.
Retaliation is barbed wire, and it is exceedingly hard to get yourself untangled from it once it is perceived to occur.

t: Am I Cool With Teachers Asking AI to Pretend Its Me
q: Rick isn’t the first person I’ve heard of doing this because I’ve done it myself. Yep. I’ve asked AI to pretend it’s me and give me advice from my perspective.

asking AI to pretend it’s me doesn’t enact a theft of my intellectual property. That theft has already taken place. The most up-to-date AI chatbots — e.g., Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and so on — have all been trained on basically the entire internet.
I’m not worried about it from the intellectual property angle; I’m just one of millions of creators whose work has been used in this matter, absent our permission.

Nothing has helped my practice more than writing about it. And Rick’s message attests to the success of the second — my work has been helpful to him. My writing has done for Rick what the writing of others (e.g., Jim Burke, Mike Schmoker, Kelly Gallagher, Penny Kittle) has done for me: it has behaved like a mentor.

if asking AI to pretend it’s me can help you in your work as an educator, I have no real qualms with it. There are, of course, the general qualms that come with any use of AI: it can only add to the understanding you already have; it can be wrong, in all sorts of ways; it can quickly become a crutch; it has environmental costs.

These tools have taken their toll on the creator economy in that they’ve radically reduced web traffic to creator websites and the appertaining revenue such traffic provides creators with. I’ve seen bot traffic to the server my site is hosted on explode and human traffic dwindle.

t: Retaining the Talents of 'Ready Now' Leaders
q: The best organizations are highly thoughtful about the development opportunities for leaders on the runway toward a bigger role, but they often scratch their heads when it comes to Ready Now leaders waiting for a top job to open up.
Senior roles and positions are typically hard to come by in most organizations, so there are usually more Ready Now candidates sitting in the queue than is ideal.
By having units, divisions, groups, and functions led by two people, organizations double the opportunities for Ready Now leaders.
Increasingly popular is for organizations to create a developmental role for 18-24 months where Ready Now leaders can see the organization from a different vantage and get themselves set.
A succession plan without a talent retention strategy for Ready Now leaders isn’t much of a plan at all.

t: Research Bite #36: Students ignore their mistakes
q: This scholarly article explores how secondary school students interact with error feedback in a digital German grammar learning application.

The study analyzed over 20,000 assessment cases from a real-world educational setting, revealing that prior knowledge significantly impacts feedback engagement, with higher-achieving students being more likely to seek and appreciate feedback.
Students with low prior knowledge are less likely to seek and engage with elaborated error feedback, despite being the group who could benefit from it the most.

While these students could benefit the most from such detailed feedback to close knowledge gaps, they are paradoxically less likely to seek, comprehend, and perceive its usefulness, often ignoring it entirely.

Low formative assessment scores, indicating low prior knowledge, are strongly associated with reduced error feedback seeking and error feedback comprehension, as well as a more critical perspective on error feedback usefulness.
Teachers should monitor student engagement and provide targeted support to help them utilize feedback effectively.

t: Our Relationship With Others Depends First on Our Relationship With Ourselves
q: As a rule, our external relationships reflect our internal state.
Self-trust, self-respect, and self-awareness form the core foundation for all genuine relationships.

On the other hand, negative self-talk, such as self-criticism, doubt, admonishment, and distorted thinking (like “always” and “never”), harms relationships by creating barriers, weakening conviction, and fueling misunderstandings.
Unhappiness on the inside produces unhappiness on the outside. That’s why our relationship with others depends enormously on our relationship with ourselves.
Examine your self-talk and the feelings you have about yourself. Perhaps it’s time for a tune-up.

t: Leaders Who Hijack Meetings
q: It’s common for high-energy and passionate storytellers to have a recency bias. They want to tell others about whatever has most excited them lately.
Unknowingly, they take conversations and discussions off track by introducing their most recent breakthrough from the first moment in a meeting.
Many leaders with this weakness often don’t realize they do this and generally can’t stop themselves, even when they are aware.
The better choice is to set a strong and clear agenda and then to remind everyone that there will be time at the end to discuss recent developments and insights.
A leader’s passion to share their insights is a good thing until it overrides what needs to get done and discussed. Then that passion needs a lid.

t: The Impact of Compressing Timelines
q: Parkinson’s Law suggests that work always expands to fill the time available to do it.
As a rule, when any deadline and the consequences of not fulfilling it loom near, attention becomes laser-focused and full of intensity.
People get incredibly creative when timelines become compressed. Innovation typically skyrockets when leaders set near-impossible timelines.
Contracting timelines too frequently will likely contribute to burnout, stress, and dissatisfaction.
If you have all day to do the job, it will probably take you the whole day, but if you only have two hours, you will find a way to do it in two hours.

t: Bookletising the Curriculum
q: My initial goals were clear: to purposefully embed two key teaching approaches - the area model for multiplication and algebraic expansion and the use of two-coloured counters - from the outset.

This led to the creation of "calculating the LBHS way" – a unit designed not just to teach content, but to introduce both students and staff to our fundamental approach to calculation, and ultimately, to facilitate this broader access to Stage 7.
Crucially, we actively discourage rote reliance on "BIDMAS", instead fostering a deeper understanding of mathematical operations.
What we actually found was that if we implemented highly planned checks for understanding and thorough prerequisite checks, we could support significantly more classes.
Ultimately, we ended up with four classes out of six in Year 7 studying Stage 7, quadrupling what we had the year before.
There's no denying that the workload and pressure to produce these units have been considerable. However, seeing the payoff has been immensely rewarding.

t: AI in Schools: Three Things to Get Right
q: AI is best understood as a “General Purpose Technology”, akin to steam power, electricity, or the internet, except it is unfolding at a much faster pace and at the level of cognition rather than mechanics.

I get the sense that ahead of the new school year, some schools are working with AI-generated curricula which are effectively plastic plants: they may look convincing on the surface but lack the roots, depth, and vitality of real curricula developed by expert teachers.

Schools need subject specific curriculum teams, not just IT departments, leading AI procurement decisions. The key question isn't "Does this AI system work?" but "Does it understand our subject the way our best teachers do?
Many of these personalised systems have tracked right/wrong answers but then failed to capture why a student is struggling and more importantly, what to do about it.
This keeps teachers as the arbiters of quality while AI handles the legwork, delivering comparable scores and feedback with far less time than traditional marking.
As Dylan Wiliam recently cautioned, AI tools may help with logistics like scoring or collating, but “there are limitations to AI's feedback and assessment capabilities”.

t: 3-Read Friday #81: Back to School Resources, AI in Schools, and Bookletising the Curriculum
q: Colleen is one of the OG maths bloggers and is still going strong. In this post, she compiles a wealth of lovely resources to use with students during the first few weeks and throughout the coming year.

I am fascinated by the impact AI is having, and will have, on our jobs and the education of our students. Carl addresses three key aspects of AI that teachers and leaders need to consider as the world around us rapidly changes.
Booklets, PowerPoints and departmental approaches to topics have been regular themes in my newsletters and podcasts over the last few years, and always divide opinion.
I loved reading Jon’s endeavours to develop a coherent approach across his maths department to two key topics.
Primary teachers, have you seen our brand-new White Rose maths collection of diagnostic questions? Reception to Year 6, all free, available here.

t: The Unpacking Principle in Relationships
q: The Unpacking Principle suggests that the more detailed and specific information a leader or practitioner compiles, the more likely they are to understand the problem and devise a creative plan to address it.
History and knowledge about each other create the foundation for this expansion. The more the parties unpack and explore who they are, the more likely it is for trust and affiliation to prosper.
The disclosure associated with a person’s history and backstory is very different from knowing their preferences and hobbies.
So instead of asking new relationships what they do or where they are from, perhaps the stronger question is, “What is your story?
The history you don’t know can stand as a roadblock to a beautiful union.

t: Mini-Sermonizing Academic Integrity
q: I thought there was something universal happening here related to a mid-year slump. So I set out to re-center our purpose and also clarify my expectations.

it’s natural to lose sight of those intrinsic goals as time goes on and shift to “just getting by” — trying to pass the quiz, get the homework done, etc. But working like that won’t actually improve our skills.
They seemed a little wide-eyed to see it spelled out so directly, and someone said, “No, that covers it” and we laughed.
they were visibly moved by my suggestion that above all else they give themselves some grace.

I think it built trust that I named the behaviors directly, and set us up for less strife in the future now that my expectations are super clear. They know what happens if they cheat, but they also know I won’t think they are a bad person.
I could see a number of them really benefited from being reminded that they do value improving their skills, and they want to leave this class stronger readers, writers, and thinkers.

t: Strategies to Cope With Larger Teams and More Direct Reports Than Ever Before
q: The ratio of managers to team members has increased dramatically in just a couple of years, with managers in many organizations asked to oversee as many as 15-20 direct reports.
With an ever-expanding number of direct reports, leaders no longer have the time to coach, guide, nurture, nudge, and mentor team members.
Because they are no longer on top of what team members are doing, problems that arise can catch leaders by surprise and are often beyond repair.
Instituting “office hours” where team members can rely on a set time to bring issues to the forefront and receive the guidance they need is another strategy worth considering.
How leaders spend their time defines their leadership. Making the time for those you lead is the highest calling and always will be.

t: The Difference Between Motivation and Inspiration and Why It Matters
q: Motivation is anything that compels a person to action. Fueled by what we want or need, we are motivated to attain what we desire or to avoid what we don’t.

Inspiration is anything that lights the fire or amplifies the desire to act. The inspirational urge to act is not to gain or avoid outcomes but to behave consistently with our most deeply held values and beliefs.

They are motivated to exercise because they want to improve their health, look better, and receive praise from others. They are inspired to exercise after hearing a story that resonates emotionally and suggests they are not living up to their full potential physically.
Too many leaders overly depend on incentives like compensation to motivate team members, with little attention to other tools or the need to inspire higher performance.
Leaders who motivate by lighting a fire underneath people are never as effective as those who also light the fire within them.

t: Bad Goals Dressed as Good Ones
q: A lot of times, the students who present as highly motivated in school are actually very poorly motivated for learning.
They are scarce. Each of these goals requires students to compete for limited spots. This increases pressure on students, often past what is optimal.

They emphasize and external locus of control. What I mean is, success at these goals depends to a large degree on factors outside an individual student’s influence rather than their own actions and choices.
Goals like this tend to blind us toward the beauty and power of today. Always looking to the future is a sad way to live. Ask a guy who had to learn this the hard way!

When things are going their way, sure — they’ll present as motivated for the work of learning. But this motivation will be hollow because they’ll be doing the work for where it gets them and not for the work’s inherent Value.

It takes careful, consistent heart-gardening on the part of teachers. It takes a light touch, too. We don’t want to denigrate goals like this because, c’mon — these are hard things to accomplish and we do hard things!
learning, fundamentally, is about exploring the cosmos and becoming a human.

t: The Need for Closure Can Lead to Faulty Decisions
q: The need for closure is a psychological drive to find definite answers and conclusions and to avoid ambiguity.
When leaders and decision-makers feel a strong need for closure, they reduce their consideration of new information and plausible alternatives.
Leaders who value control, structure, and routine tend to have a higher need for closure, often feeling distressed by uncertainty.
The awareness that internal or external pressures exist to make a decision quickly should set off alarm bells. Relief is always a dead giveaway.

Leaders succumb to the need for closure more often than they realize. That’s because escaping the discomfort and uncertainty created by decisions can distort objectivity and convince leaders that they have sound reasons for fast closure.

t: Research Bite #35: The boy paradox: exploring motivational factors in gender differences and academic achievement across ages 9–14 years
q: This article investigates the motivational factors influencing gender differences and academic achievement in Swedish compulsory schools, particularly focusing on students aged 9-14.

Student motivation, particularly for boys, declines significantly between ages 9–12, coinciding with the introduction of grades. Teachers should foster autonomy-supportive environments and provide structured guidance.
The boy paradox: Boys report more positive perceptions of the learning environment despite generally lower academic performance.

However, teachers should be aware that boys might perceive feedback more negatively than girls. Teachers could provide more immediate and concrete feedback, while girls may respond better to nuanced, process-oriented feedback.
The current findings suggest a paradox: boys report positive perceptions despite experiencing underachievement, which may challenge existing assumptions about gendered motivation
